mcqs.question: Why is the Shape/Circle/Square hierarchy shown here a genuinely clean use of inheritance?
options: It's a closed, known set of shapes that all honor one real shared invariant (area() >= 0), with no variant needing to weaken that promise
Because abstract classes are always preferable to interfaces for shapes
Because Circle and Square have the same number of fields
Because inheritance is always the right choice when there are exactly two subclasses
mcqs.explanation: The hierarchy is closed and every subtype honors the same real invariant with no weakened promise — the actual signal for a clean fit. Field count and subclass count are irrelevant, and abstract-class-vs-interface is a separate design axis.

mcqs.question: Per the decision table, which signal points toward composition over inheritance?
options: A closed, known set of subtypes
One shared invariant every subtype honors
Two or more independent variation axes that need to combine
Is-a holding true for every subtype
mcqs.explanation: Multiple independent axes combining is exactly the signal that favors composition, since inheritance would force a subclass per combination. The other three options describe the conditions where inheritance is the cleaner fit instead.

mcqs.question: What does the Liskov substitution principle add to the informal is-a test?
options: It formalizes is-a into a checkable rule: a subtype can't strengthen a precondition or weaken a postcondition the parent promised
It requires every subclass to override every parent method
It only applies to abstract classes, not interfaces
mcqs.explanation: LSP turns the intuitive is-a check into a concrete, applicable rule about preconditions and postconditions. It doesn't ban multiple inheritance, require overriding everything, or restrict itself to abstract classes over interfaces.

mcqs.question: Why is "inheritance is fine anywhere the types are related" a wrong bar to use?
options: Because related types should always use composition instead
Because inheritance requires identical field counts between parent and child
Because relatedness can only be established through interfaces, not classes
Relatedness is a weaker test than is-a — two related types can still fail is-a if the subtype can't honor every promise the parent makes
mcqs.explanation: Relatedness doesn't check whether the subtype honors every one of the parent's promises, which is exactly what is-a (and LSP) checks. Field counts and interfaces-vs-classes have nothing to do with the relatedness trap.
